Ojingeo Gui Spicy Grilled Squid

Ojingeo gui is whole grilled squid, Korea's pojangmacha (street tent) and drinking-table classic: one squid, scored, rushed over charcoal, brushed with a sweet-spicy gochujang glaze in the last minutes, cut into rings at the…

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: restaurant — the street-and-tavern grill. Ojingeo gui is whole grilled squid, Korea's pojangmacha (street tent) and drinking-table classic: one squid, scored, rushed over charcoal, brushed with a sweet-spicy gochujang glaze in the last minutes, cut into rings at the table, and eaten with the dipping sauce and cold beer or soju that the dish was engineered to sell. It looks like restaurant theater and cooks like a technique lesson — squid has exactly one doneness question (2 minutes or 2 hours, nothing between), and this record is a masterclass in the fast answer.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Score the bodies — inside faces. Lay each body open flat (it is a tube; cut along one side and open it like a book). Score the inner face in a diagonal crosshatch, 5 mm apart, shallow cuts only — the blade should never go through. Two things happen on the fire: the scored faces curl and open into blossoms, and the increased surface area catches glaze and char. Leave the outer face smooth.
  • Dry the squid thoroughly with paper towel. Squid carries water and that water is the enemy of char; a wet squid boils gray in its own steam before it can toast.
  • Make the glaze and the dip before the fire. Whisk the glaze smooth and set it at the grill station with a brush; stir the dip together and park it on the table — the squid's speed at the end leaves no time for assembly.
  • Fire hot, with distance control: charcoal burned to gray-edge with the grate close (a palm's count of 2 seconds above the coals, roughly 250 °C at the surface), and the option to raise it.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Dry-grill first, glaze second. The scored bodies go on scored-face-down over the hot fire, tentacles beside them. Ninety seconds undisturbed — the bodies will curl and the scores will gape open, toasting in their grooves; the tentacle tips will char at their edges. Checkpoint — the scored face shows toasted brown in the grooves with light char at the curling edges; the smell is sweet-iodine ocean toast (this is correct — squid's smell on fire should be oceanic, never sulfurous; a sulfurous fish-market smell means the squid was past its day). If the bodies stick, the grate was not hot enough — a hot grate releases squid the way it releases skin.
  2. 02
    Flip, glaze, finish. Turn the bodies and tentacles, brush the toasted faces with glaze, 45–60 seconds more, and a second thin brush-stroke over each. The glaze needs only to set glossy — it is not cooking, it is dressing. Checkpoint — the glaze foams lightly and turns brick-glossy. Pull the bodies when they are just firm to the touch — springy with give, not tight as a drum. Tight-as-drum is the rubber door, and it closes at about the four-minute mark for bodies this size.
  3. 03
    Cut at the table. The scissors are the service: bodies crosswise into wide rings (the scored blossoms open as you cut), tentacles in halves. Straight from the board into the dip, or over rice with the glaze's drippings. Checkpoint — eating test, a ring straight from the dip: snap-tender bite (the 2-minute squid's signature), char in the score grooves, the glaze's sweet-heat, the dip's vinegar and chili behind it. Any rubbery chew means some piece crossed the doneness line — pull earlier next batch; squid cannot be saved, only timed. Chef’s Note — buying squid: fresh whole squid should smell of clean ocean, feel slick-but-firm, and show skin that peels easily. If you can only find cleaned frozen bodies, they work — thaw slowly, dry doubly (frozen squid carries more water), and the record proceeds. Frozen pre-scored "grill-ready" squid skips the knife lesson but costs you the curl control; scoring your own lets you cut deeper over a smaller area for a tighter blossom.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The squid: cleaned, skinned, inner-face crosshatch at 5 mm, bone-dry before the fire.
  • The grill: hot and close (about 250 °C at the surface), dry sear first, glaze after the flip only.
  • The pull: scored face toasted, glaze glossy, body springy-with-give before the four-minute mark.
  • The table: scissors to rings, dip ready before the fire, cold drinks standing by — the dish's whole grammar.

Finish & Plate

The whole cut squid goes to the table's center on a warm board, rings and tentacles mixed, the dip bowl beside, radish batons and rice in reach. The last tentacle goes to whoever lost count of the soja glasses; the street-tent rule is the oldest rule.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Rubbery ringsCrossed the doneness line90 + 60 seconds; pull at springy-with-give
Squid welded to the grateGrate not hot or squid wetFull preheat; dry with paper towel twice
Glaze burnt, bitterGlazed before the flipDry sear first; glaze sets in 45 seconds
Scores did not openCut too shallow or outer-face scoredInner face, 5 mm crosshatch, blade shallow
Sulfur smell on the fireSquid past its dayNothing recovers it; buy fresher

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Raw squid keeps 1 day on ice; glaze and dip keep a week (the dip improves). Cooked rings keep 1 day and make a fierce stir-fried rice or noodle addition, reheated hard and fast — remember, this record is the 2-minute pole of squid's doneness law; the 2-hour pole is a different dish entirely (braised ojingeo-jjim, not this record).
  • Variations: the clean-lane fork skips the glaze for soy-garlic baste and the #SF02 register; baby octopus runs this same glaze on the jjukkumi record (#SF06); the dip doubles as the sauce for cold boiled eggs, a pojangmacha two-fer.
